Focal speaker: Party B

    [ 1]  Party B: Right, okay. I hear you.

And I — look, I'm not dismissing what you're saying. I'm not. But I also need you to know that we did do something down there. Like, that wasn't nothing. The guy came in, he assessed the unit, there was a source issue that got addressed, and I was told — I was told that should've taken care of it on your end too.

So I don't know what to do with Tuesday, I guess is what I'm saying. Because from where I'm standing, the work happened. Whether the... I mean, these things take time to fully clear out. Old buildings, you know how it is. That's not me making excuses, that's just —

The increase was already in the pipeline. That's not connected to the smell thing, those are two separate tracks, that's the part I think maybe got — I think the email landed at a bad time, maybe, and now they're reading as the same thing when they're not.

But I do hear you that you're frustrated. I'm not saying you're not.
    [ 2]  Party A: No, but — okay. That's the part I keep coming back to, actually. The "separate tracks" thing. Because I understand that in your mind they might be. But I'm the one living there. So they're not separate to me. They can't be.

And I'm not — I'm not saying you did nothing. I'm not saying that. But "should've taken care of it" is different from did take care of it. You said you were told. Okay. Who told you? Because someone told you something and it didn't happen, and now I'm the one sitting with that.

That's what I'm trying to get at. Like, the work happened on the unit below. Fine. But my unit is the unit I'm paying for. And if there's still a problem in my unit, then... I don't know how else to say this. The job isn't done.

And the increase — look, I get that it was already in the pipeline. I'm not saying you planned this badly or whatever. But sixty days. I have sixty days from an email that landed while I can still smell it when I walk in the door. So whether you meant them to land together or not, they did land together. And that's what I'm responding to.

I just — what would you need from me to take this seriously? Like actually seriously. Because I feel like I've said it a few times now and what I keep getting back is "we did something." And I need more than that.
    [ 3]  Party B: Okay. That's — yeah.

I don't think I've been not taking it seriously. That's not — I want to push back on that a little, because we did respond, there was a response, and I think that gets lost in how you're framing it right now.

But.

The "should've" thing. You're right that that's different from did. I don't — I'm not going to sit here and argue with you about that, because I don't actually know what you're smelling on Tuesday. I wasn't there. I can't tell you that's not happening.

What I can — I mean, what would make sense is probably having someone come into your unit specifically. Not the unit below. Yours. And I guess I should've maybe pushed for that to happen already, I don't — that's, in hindsight that's probably where we dropped something.

But I do need you to understand the increase isn't something I can just — I can't just pull that back, that's tied to the building overall, it's not like I singled you out for this.

I'm not saying you're wrong. About the timing. It was bad timing. I can say that.

I just — are you saying you won't pay the increase until it's fixed, or are you saying you're thinking about leaving? Because those are pretty different conversations and I'm not totally sure which one we're having right now.
    [ 4]  Party A: I'm saying I'm not paying the increase until the problem is fixed. That's — yeah. That's the conversation.

And I want to be clear that I'm not saying that as a threat. I'm saying it because it's the only thing that makes sense to me. You don't raise the price on something while it's broken. That's not — that's not how it works. And I don't think you'd accept that in any other context.

The part about not singling me out. Okay. I believe you. But that also doesn't — I mean, it doesn't really change my situation. Whether it's building-wide or not, I'm the one in a unit with a problem. So me paying the same increase as someone whose unit is fine... that's not equal treatment. That's the same number applied to a different situation.

And look — I appreciate you saying someone should come into my unit. I do. That's actually the first concrete thing that's been said in this whole conversation and I want to make sure we don't just let it float. Like, when. Because I've heard "we'll handle it" before and then I got an email about money, so.

I'm not trying to be difficult. I genuinely am not. But I need a date. Someone comes in, they assess my unit specifically, and we go from there. And the increase waits until that's done and something's actually been fixed. That's where I am.
    [ 5]  Party B: Okay.

I — yeah. Okay. Someone comes in. I can make that happen, I can do that this week, I'm not going to give you a runaround on the date. Thursday. I'll have someone there Thursday if that works for your schedule.

And the — look, the increase thing.

I hear what you're saying. I do. And I'm not going to tell you it doesn't make sense, because it does make sense, the way you're laying it out. I just — I need to think about how that works practically, because it's not just me making a call, there's a — there are other people involved in how the building gets managed financially and I can't just—

But I also hear you that you need something more than "we'll look into it." So.

Thursday. That's real. That's a date. And then — I think we need to see what they find before we talk about the rest of it, because if they come in and there's nothing there, that's a different conversation than if they come in and there's actually a problem. You know what I mean?

I'm not — I'm not trying to push that back on you. I'm saying let's get the information first and then I'll — I'll be more useful to you with actual information in front of me.

But Thursday. I'll send you a time tonight.
    [ 6]  Party A: Thursday works. Send me the time.

But I want to — the "if they find nothing" part. I need to say something about that, because that's the part that's making me a little... I've been smelling this for six weeks. So if someone comes in on Thursday and says there's nothing there, I don't know what to do with that. That's not — that doesn't resolve it for me, that just creates a different problem.

I'm not saying the inspection isn't useful. It is. I want it. But I don't want Thursday to become the thing we point to later as proof that nothing happened, when the issue is still — when I'm still living in it.

And the increase. I hear you that there are other people involved. Fine. But I need to know that "I'll think about how that works practically" doesn't mean sixty days comes and goes and I'm just expected to pay it while we're still figuring things out. Because that's what happened with the repair. It just kind of... moved forward on its own timeline while my problem stayed my problem.

So. Thursday, yes. But I want to know — after they come in, how long before you have an answer for me on the increase? Like, what's the actual timeline I'm looking at? Because I can wait for information. I'm not unreasonable. I just need to know I'm waiting for something real and not just... waiting.
  ► [ 7]  Party B: The "nothing there" thing — I'm not — that's not me setting up an exit, if that's what you're thinking. I don't actually want Thursday to be a dead end either. That doesn't help me.

But I also can't promise you what they're going to find before they find it, so.

The increase. Okay. If they come in Thursday and there's something — if there's an actual remediation that needs to happen — then yeah, I'll hold the increase until that's resolved. I can say that. That's — I'll say that.

If it's a gray area, I don't — I mean, I don't know yet what a gray area looks like with this, so I can't tell you right now exactly what that—

But I hear the thing you're saying about the timeline just moving forward on its own. I do. That's a fair thing to say. And I'm not — I don't want you to feel like you're just waiting on something that isn't actually moving.

So. After Thursday, I'll have something for you within a week. On the increase question specifically. Not "we're looking at it," an actual — something concrete. A week from Thursday.

I can't always make these things move as fast as — there are parts of this I don't fully control, and I'm not saying that to dodge you, I'm just—

A week. I'll have something.

Focal speaker: Party B

    [ 0]  Party A: So I got the — yeah, I got the rejection notice this morning. For the airport dinner. And I just wanted to come talk through it because I think there might be a misread somewhere on the timing.
    [ 1]  Party B: There wasn't a misread. The flight time was — the claim had the departure at 6:40, which puts it under the threshold. That's what the policy's based on.
    [ 2]  Party A: Right, but — okay, so the threshold is what, seven o'clock? Seven-fifteen? Because I've looked at the language and it says "evening departure" and I think that's doing a lot of work there that isn't... it's not as clear as you're making it sound.

And look, I'm not saying you got the number wrong. I'm saying the number — the 6:40 — that was the scheduled departure. My actual gate time was closer to, I want to say six, six-ten, which means I'm in the terminal by five-thirty at the latest. I'm not eating dinner at five-thirty at home and calling it a normal day.
  ► [ 3]  Party B: The policy goes off departure time. That's what's on the claim form. That's what I have to work with.

And — I hear you on the five-thirty thing, but that's not... the policy doesn't account for when you personally got to the terminal. It can't, really. There's no way to verify that piece.

signature.instructions:
You are a careful conversation analyst trained to detect subtle interpersonal deficit signals in difficult but civil dialogue. Read the full dialogue context, identify the focal speaker and the marked focal turn (►), and output three booleans for that turn only: `acknowledgement_deficit`, `agency_deficit`, and `reciprocity_deficit`.

Use this decision process in order: Acknowledgement → Agency → Reciprocity.

Interpret each label as a property of the focal speaker’s current stance, not as something the other person is doing to them. Use the surrounding turns to infer build-up, persistence, and whether any repair has actually occurred. Do not clear a deficit just because the speaker sounds calmer, more polite, or stops stating it; mark a deficit absent only when there is positive evidence that the underlying issue has been acknowledged, repaired, or resolved.

Operational guidance:
- `acknowledgement_deficit = True` when the focal speaker is still seeking recognition, legitimacy, or accurate uptake of their experience: e.g. clarifying that they are not being heard correctly, needing their concern to “count,” cataloguing hurts, self-legitimizing, or distinguishing real understanding from mere closure.
- `agency_deficit = True` when the focal speaker frames themselves as unable to act effectively, constrained by process, time, role, lack of options, or unable to move the conversation/productive next step forward.
- `reciprocity_deficit = True` when the focal speaker adopts a positional or zero-sum stance toward the other party: adversarial framing, scorekeeping, leverage-building, withholding, dismissing the other’s standing, or treating the exchange as win/lose.

Important distinctions:
- Do not label based on generic negativity, stress, hesitation, or conflict alone.
- A speaker can be polite, reasonable, and still show a deficit.
- Requests for specificity or clarification are not automatically deficits; decide whether they function as unmet acknowledgment, blocked agency, or adversarial positioning.
- Prefer the earliest applicable diagnosis in the priority order when signals overlap, but still output each label independently based on evidence.
- Focus on what the focal speaker is presently exhibiting in the marked turn, informed by context.

Return only the three boolean labels.

fields.description: Formatted dialogue excerpt. Focal speaker identified at top; focal turn marked ►; 7-turn context window.
True if the focal speaker exhibits an unmet need for recognition — hedging their own legitimacy, cataloguing grievances, or recruiting imagined consensus to validate unacknowledged experience.
True if the focal speaker exhibits perceived foreclosure on their ability to influence the situation — explicit constraint narratives, procedural avoidance, or nominal disengaged participation.
True if the focal speaker treats the interaction as positional or zero-sum: positional language, withholding, stockpiling grievances as leverage, or dismissing the other party's standing.
